record.paper_title: Open questions on the impact of an inflated ball
record.original_question: How should the regulated inflation pressure of a sports ball be chosen so that the ball's impact mechanics produce a game that is fast and entertaining while still limiting single-impact or repetitive-impact injury risk? The question requires relating inflation pressure to ball impact behavior before deciding whether the observed sport-specific pressure ranges reflect a fun-versus-risk trade-off.

evidence.quote: The sports balls are all submitted to specific game rules. For every sport, the rules of the game strictly bound the inflation pressure. Why is it so? This question is not straight forward, since sports rules were built by usage.

An hypothesis for the convergence value for inflation pressure could be a fun/risk trade-off. One may think that in the one hand, the sport might be fast to be entertaining which requires large inflation pressure. In the other hand, if the ball is too much inflated it induces injuries after one single or repetitive impacts, which may prevent largest inflation pressures. However, to answer this hypothesis, one has to understand first how does the ball behaves during an impact: what is the impact mechanics of an inflated ball?

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider a thin-walled elastic spherical shell of radius $R$, wall thickness $h$, made of a material with Young's modulus $E$ and Poisson ratio $
u$, inflated with an internal gauge pressure $P$ (so that the absolute internal pressure is $P_0+P$ with $P_0$ the ambient atmospheric pressure). The ball, of total mass $m$, strikes a rigid flat surface (or is struck by a rigid flat striker) at normal incidence with speed $v$.

(a) Derive a quantitative model of the impact mechanics that expresses, in terms of $(R,h,E,
u,P,P_0,m,v)$, the following observables: the contact time $	au(P)$, the maximum contact force $F_{\max}(P)$, the maximum local deformation (flattening) $\delta_{\max}(P)$, the coefficient of restitution $e(P)$, and the rebound speed $v'(P)=e(P)\,v$.

(b) Define a "speed-of-play" functional $S(P)$ that increases with the rebound speed and/or with $1/	au(P)$, and an "injury-risk" functional $I(P)$ that increases with the peak force $F_{\max}(P)$ (single-impact risk) and with a cumulative-loading measure $\int F(t)^\alpha\,dt$ over repeated impacts (for some exponent $\alpha\ge 1$ characterizing tissue damage). Formulate and solve the optimization problem of choosing $P$ so as to maximize a trade-off objective $U(P)=S(P)-\lambda\,I(P)$, with $\lambda>0$.

(c) Determine whether the optimal pressure $P^\star(\lambda)$ obtained from this fun-versus-risk trade-off, when specialized to the parameters $(R,h,E,
u,m)$ of common sports balls (e.g.\ basketball, volleyball, soccer, handball, tennis), agrees quantitatively with the regulated pressure ranges fixed by the official rules of those sports.

Provide either an explicit derivation establishing this agreement, or a counterexample showing that the regulated ranges cannot be explained by such a trade-off.
artifact.status_search_result: The problem is posed as an open question about the physical mechanics of inflated-ball impacts and whether regulated sport pressure ranges arise from a fun/risk optimum. While partial impact-mechanics models for inflated balls (e.g., membrane-pressure-dominated regimes) have appeared in subsequent sports-physics literature, no published work appears to close the optimization-and-comparison loop across sports to confirm the trade-off hypothesis. Status appears open.

status_evidence.title: Open questions on the impact of an inflated ball
status_evidence.snippet: Discusses regulated inflation pressures in sports and proposes a fun/risk trade-off hypothesis as an open question, contingent on first understanding inflated-ball impact mechanics.
status_evidence.claim: The fun-versus-risk trade-off explanation for regulated inflation pressures is explicitly stated as an open question.
